title: Home
text:
Hi, I’m Christa Ingabire. I’m currently pursuing a Master’s in Data Science at the University of British Columbia.
Before graduate school, I worked as a data engineer at the Rwanda Social Security Board in Kigali, where I built and maintained data pipelines supporting national social protection programs. Before that, I worked in software and data consulting in Minneapolis.
My interests sit at the intersection of data engineering, statistical learning, machine learning, and applied data science, particularly when data represents people, institutions, and public systems.
This site is a collection of computational work, technical notes, and occasional writing as I develop those interests further.

title: Passing Data Between R and Python
text:
This post explores how R and Python can work together using reticulate. I create data in R, use it in Python, and then bring a Python result back into R for visualization.
First, I create a small data frame in R.

library(reticulate)
use_python(Sys.which("python"), required = TRUE)

practice <- data.frame(
  language = c("Python", "R", "SQL"),
  hours = c(8, 5, 6)
)

practice

  language hours
1   Python     8
2        R     5
3      SQL     6


Next, Python reads the R object using r.practice and calculates the number of minutes practiced.

practice_from_r = r.practice
practice_from_r

  language  hours
0   Python    8.0
1        R    5.0
2      SQL    6.0


Back in R, I ask Python to perform the calculation in its main session. The result can then be accessed from R using py$minutes.

py_run_string("
practice_from_r = r.practice
minutes = practice_from_r['hours'] * 60
")

practice$minutes <- py$minutes

practice

  language hours minutes
1   Python     8     480
2        R     5     300
3      SQL     6     360


The original data was created in R, Python calculated the new minutes values, and R retrieved the Python result.
Finally, I use those values to create a simple graph in R.

barplot(
  practice$minutes,
  names.arg = practice$language,
  xlab = "Language",
  ylab = "Practice time (minutes)"
)







Figure 1: Practice time by programming language, with minutes calculated in Python.





This demonstrates data moving between the two languages. Python accessed the R object through r.practice, and R accessed a result created in Python through py$minutes.

title: My First Weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day on campus.
There is something strange about becoming a student again after spending a few years working full-time.
Before coming to Vancouver, I was working as a data engineer in Kigali. My days revolved around production data, pipelines, databases, and the practical constraints that come with maintaining systems other people depend on. Now I am back in a classroom, beginning a Master’s in Data Science and returning to subjects I have not studied formally in several years.

title: My First Weeks in MDS
text:
Starting again
My first few days at UBC were a combination of finding buildings, meeting people whose names I was trying very hard to remember, and slowly realizing how much I am going to have to learn this year.
Returning to school after working feels different from starting university for the first time. I have more context now for why certain things matter. Concepts that once felt abstract are easier to connect to problems I have encountered at work.
At the same time, there are foundations I need to rebuild.
Working in industry taught me how to solve particular problems, but familiarity with tools is not the same as understanding the ideas underneath them. One of my goals this year is to become more deliberate about that distinction.

title: My First Weeks in MDS
section: From building systems to asking questions
text:
From building systems to asking questions
A large part of my professional experience has been on the infrastructure side of data: getting information where it needs to go, making it reliable, and making it usable.
That work also left me with questions that infrastructure alone cannot answer.
It is one thing to build a pipeline that accurately reports a change in some outcome. It is another to understand why that change occurred, whether an observed relationship is meaningful, or how confidently we can generalize from the data we have.
That gap is part of what brought me back to school.

title: My First Weeks in MDS
text:
What I hope to learn
Over the next year, I want to strengthen my foundations in statistics and machine learning while becoming a better programmer and a more careful analyst.
I am particularly interested in learning how to move between different layers of a data problem: from the systems that produce and organize data, to the statistical assumptions behind an analysis, to the decisions that eventually get made from the result.
I expect some of that learning to be uncomfortable. There are already moments when I recognize a concept without being able to explain it as clearly as I would like. I am trying to treat those moments as useful information about what I need to revisit.
It is still early, and I do not know exactly what this year will look like. For now, I am excited to be learning again.
I plan to use this site to document some of that process: analyses, technical problems, things I misunderstood, and occasionally things that finally clicked.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins
text:
For this post, I wanted to see how some basic physical measurements differ between the three penguin species in the Palmer Penguins dataset. I focused on body mass and flipper length because both give a simple way to compare the species.
Data source: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. Data are available under a CC0 license.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins
text:
For this post, I wanted to see how some basic physical measurements differ between the three penguin species in the Palmer Penguins dataset. I focused on body mass and flipper length because both give a simple way to compare the species.
Data source: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. Data are available under a CC0 license.

Next, I checked the size of the dataset and the columns available.

Rows and columns: (344, 8)


Index(['species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'bill_depth_mm',
       'flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g', 'sex', 'year'],

There are several measurements available, but for this post I am mainly interested in species, body_mass_g, and flipper_length_mm.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins
text:
Comparing the species
I grouped the penguins by species and calculated the average body mass and flipper length for each group.

species_summary = penguins.groupby("species")[
    ["body_mass_g", "flipper_length_mm"]
].mean()

species_summary = species_summary.round(1)

species_summary

This gives me one row for each species instead of one row for each individual penguin. The differences are already pretty noticeable, especially for Gentoo penguins.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins
text:
Visualizing body mass
I used the species averages to compare body mass visually.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

species_summary["body_mass_g"].plot(
    kind="bar",
    figsize=(7, 4)
)

plt.title("Gentoo penguins are heavier on average")
plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Average body mass (g)")
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Average body mass of Palmer penguins by species.





Gentoo penguins stand out immediately. Their average body mass is much higher than the other two species, while Adelie penguins have the lowest average.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins
text:
Looking at flipper length
Since Gentoo penguins were also larger in the summary table, I wanted to look at flipper length separately.

species_summary["flipper_length_mm"].sort_values()

species
Adelie       190.0
Chinstrap    195.8
Gentoo       217.2
Name: flipper_length_mm, dtype: float64


The same general pattern appears here. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers on average, while Adelie penguins have the shortest.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins
text:
What I noticed
The species differ quite a bit in both measurements. Gentoo penguins are the heaviest of the three on average and also have the longest flippers. Adelie penguins are smaller on both measurements, with Chinstrap penguins falling between them.
This is a small analysis, but it was a useful way to see how grouping the data can make differences between categories much easier to spot.

title: Life Expectancy Across Continents
text:
For this post, I wanted to look at how life expectancy has changed across different parts of the world. I used the Gapminder dataset, which contains country-level data on life expectancy, population, and GDP per capita over several decades.
I was mainly interested in two things: how continents compare in the latest year available, and whether those differences look the same when viewed over time.
Data source: Gapminder. Free material from Gapminder, CC BY 4.0.

title: Life Expectancy Across Continents
text:
For this post, I wanted to look at how life expectancy has changed across different parts of the world. I used the Gapminder dataset, which contains country-level data on life expectancy, population, and GDP per capita over several decades.
I was mainly interested in two things: how continents compare in the latest year available, and whether those differences look the same when viewed over time.
Data source: Gapminder. Free material from Gapminder, CC BY 4.0.

title: Life Expectancy Across Continents
text:
Exploring the data
I started by loading the packages and looking at the first few rows of the dataset.

library(gapminder)
library(ggplot2)

head(gapminder)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
  <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.


Each row represents a country in a particular year. For this post, I am mostly interested in continent, year, and lifeExp

title: Life Expectancy Across Continents
text:
Comparing continents in 2007
First, I checked the latest year available in the dataset and created a smaller dataset containing only observations from that year.

latest_year <- max(gapminder$year)
latest_data <- subset(gapminder, year == latest_year)

latest_year

[1] 2007


The latest year is 2007. Next, I calculated the average life expectancy for each continent

latest_summary <- aggregate(
  lifeExp ~ continent,
  data = latest_data,
  FUN = mean
)

latest_summary

  continent  lifeExp
1    Africa 54.80604
2  Americas 73.60812
3      Asia 70.72848
4    Europe 77.64860
5   Oceania 80.71950


There is already a noticeable difference between the continents. Oceania has the highest average life expectancy in 2007, followed by Europe, while Africa has the lowest.
That made me curious about whether the gap between continents had always looked this way, so I looked at the full time period next.

title: Life Expectancy Across Continents
text:
Looking over time
To compare the trends, I calculated average life expectancy for each continent in each year.

continent_year <- aggregate(
  lifeExp ~ continent + year,
  data = gapminder,
  FUN = mean
)

head(continent_year)

  continent year  lifeExp
1    Africa 1952 39.13550
2  Americas 1952 53.27984
3      Asia 1952 46.31439
4    Europe 1952 64.40850
5   Oceania 1952 69.25500
6    Africa 1957 41.26635


Now each row represents the average for one continent in one year. I plotted those averages to make the changes easier to compare.

ggplot(
  continent_year,
  aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, color = continent)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Life expectancy has risen across every continent",
    subtitle = "Average life expectancy, 1952–2007",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Life expectancy (years)",
    color = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )







Figure 1: Average life expectancy by continent from 1952 to 2007.

title: Life Expectancy Across Continents
text:
What I noticed
The graph gives a much better picture than the 2007 averages alone. Life expectancy rises across every continent, but the paths are noticeably different.
Asia has one of the biggest changes, starting below 50 years and reaching above 70 by 2007. Europe and Oceania stay relatively high throughout the dataset, while the Americas also show a fairly steady increase.
Africa stands out because its trend is less consistent. Life expectancy rises for much of the period, but the line becomes much flatter around the 1990s and early 2000s before increasing again toward 2007.
Looking at the full timeline was more useful than only comparing the final year. The averages generally moved upward, but the differences between continents were still visible at the end of the dataset.

title: Christa Ingabire

My path into data science began in computer science. I studied computer science and business analytics at Saint Mary’s University of Minnesota before beginning my career in the Twin Cities.

title: Christa Ingabire
text:
Why data science
A reliable data pipeline can help us understand what happened. A dashboard can show where a pattern changed. But many of the questions I became interested in required going further.
Why did an outcome change? How much of that change can reasonably be attributed to a particular intervention? Would the same relationship hold for another population?
Those questions pushed my interests beyond data infrastructure toward statistics, causal inference, and machine learning.
I am now developing those foundations at UBC while continuing to explore data engineering, applied statistics, machine learning, and the design of trustworthy data systems. I am particularly interested in problems where technical decisions interact with institutions and real-world consequences.
